open-question.question: Does the extension's release skill take the version to release as an argument and write it into `package.json` and `package-lock.json` itself, as `/release-plugin` writes the plugin's, or does it release whatever version the manifest already holds after a bump made by hand?
open-question.recommendation: One required argument is the version the run validates, writes, packages, and publishes, in the call shape `/release-plugin` already has, and npm keeps the manifest and both lock-file sites in step with no script of the project's own to write and test.
open-question.alternative: The skill takes the version as a required bare `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` argument, as `/release-plugin` does. After its checks pass it writes that version into `gurita-vscode/package.json` and `package-lock.json` with `npm version <VERSION> --no-git-tag-version`, run through the nvm Node 22 wrapper inside `gurita-vscode/`. npm makes no commit and no tag, and the skill writes the version before it packages and publishes. One argument gives the version the run validates, writes, packages, and publishes, so a release can never go out at a version nobody chose for it. npm keeps the manifest and both lock-file sites in step with no code of the project's own, and the call shape matches `/release-plugin`'s. The written version rests on npm's behaviour rather than on a tested tool of the repository's, and npm must already run through nvm. The skill must also recognise a re-run in which the manifest already holds the argument, after an interrupted or half-published release, and treat it as a resumption rather than a bump to refuse. The commit that carries the write is the release-commit sibling's to settle.

The skill takes the version as a required bare `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` argument and writes it into `package.json` and both version sites of `package-lock.json` through a new tracked script of the extension's own, for example under `gurita-vscode/scripts/`. Like `scripts/set_version.py`, the script renders every surface in memory first, writes all of them or none, touches no git, and is covered by a test. `scripts/set_version.py` itself stays the plugin's alone. It mirrors how the plugin's version is written: one tested script names every surface the extension's version lives in and writes them in lockstep, so a lock file left at the old version is caught by a test rather than found in a published package. It adds code and a test to maintain for an edit npm already makes, and the script must locate the lock file's two root-package version sites itself without touching the dependency entries beside them. It shares the resumption handling a version argument needs on a re-run.

The skill takes the version as a required bare `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` argument but writes nothing before publishing. It passes the argument to `vsce publish <VERSION> --no-git-tag-version`, which writes `package.json` and `package-lock.json` through npm as part of the Marketplace publish, and then publishes to Open VSX from the manifest as written. The tree is committed only after the publish. The registry tool owns both the bump and the publish, so the skill holds no version-writing step of its own and the written version is exactly the one the Marketplace accepted. The manifest is changed only at publish time, after the confirmation and the package build, so the package the pre-flight built was built at the old version. A failure between the Marketplace publish and the Open VSX publish leaves an uncommitted manifest, which makes the half-published re-run harder. It also leaves to `vsce` a step whose commit and tag behaviour must be held off by a flag, which the release-commit and tag siblings depend on.

The skill takes no version argument. It releases whatever version `gurita-vscode/package.json` holds at `HEAD`. Before running it, the maintainer edits the manifest and lock file by hand, or runs `npm version` themselves, and commits the change as an ordinary commit. The skill writes no version anywhere and reads the release's version from the manifest. It is the smallest skill and keeps today's documented practice that the version is bumped by hand. A re-run after a half-published release needs no resumption logic for the version, because the manifest already holds the version being released. Nothing makes the maintainer choose a version at release time, so a forgotten bump runs straight into a registry's refusal of an already-published version, and a mistaken bump is published as it stands. The lock file's two sites can drift from the manifest unless a check catches it. The call shape also differs from `/release-plugin`'s, whose argument is the version.

The maintainer bumps and commits the manifest and lock file by hand before the run, as in the hand-bump option. The skill still takes a required bare `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` argument, but it uses the argument only as a confirmation: the run stops before anything is published unless `package.json` and both `package-lock.json` sites hold exactly that version. The skill writes no version itself. The maintainer states the intended version on the command line, as with `/release-plugin`, so a forgotten or mistyped bump stops the run before publishing. The skill still never edits a version file, and a re-run with the same argument is naturally a resumption. Every release costs two steps, a hand bump and commit and then the run, and the version is typed twice. Its protection comes from the stop rather than from the skill making the bump, so the hand edit of the lock file stays a chore.

The skill takes a bump kind, `major`, `minor`, or `patch`, instead of a version literal. It computes the next version from the one `package.json` holds and writes it into `package.json` and `package-lock.json` itself, through `npm version <kind> --no-git-tag-version` or a tracked script, before packaging and publishing. The maintainer never types a version number, so a typo or a skipped or repeated number cannot reach a registry, and the next version always follows from the last one in the manifest. The argument differs in form from `/release-plugin`'s literal version. A re-run after a half-published release cannot pass the same argument again without bumping a second time, so resumption needs a separate form. Whether a single bump from the manifest's current `0.1.0` reaches the first publication's number depends on the first-published-version sibling.

The skill accepts a bare `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` argument but does not require it. Given one, it writes that version into `package.json` and `package-lock.json` itself before packaging and publishing. Given none, it releases the version the manifest already holds, which may have been bumped and committed by hand. It serves both habits: a one-step release at a typed version, or a release of a bump already made and reviewed in its own commit. A re-run after a half-published release can simply omit the argument. The skill has two paths to document and keep correct. A run without an argument loses the protection of a stated version, so a forgotten bump is caught only by a registry's refusal or by a check the pre-flight sibling may or may not include.

open-question.question: `gurita-vscode/` holds no changelog, and the root `CHANGELOG.md` holds the plugin's release notes. Does the extension get a changelog of its own, which the package would carry to both listings, and in which file?
open-question.recommendation: `vsce` packages a `CHANGELOG.md` at the extension root with no flag, so both listings show the extension's own history on their changelog tabs, and the root changelog, whose headings `/release-plugin` counts and extracts by version, stays the plugin's alone.
open-question.alternative: The extension gets a changelog of its own, a tracked `gurita-vscode/CHANGELOG.md` holding one entry per extension release, newest first. It sits at the extension root where `vsce package` picks it up by name with no flag, so the VSIX carries it and both the Marketplace and Open VSX show it on their changelog tabs. The root `CHANGELOG.md` stays the plugin's release notes only, and `/release-plugin` is not changed. The two products keep separate histories, each in the file its own tooling expects. The listings show the extension's own changes. `/release-plugin`'s `## <VERSION> — ` heading count and its extraction from `HEAD:CHANGELOG.md` cannot collide with an extension version, and adding the file changes nothing in the build beyond one more file in the package. The repository holds a second file that must be written at every extension release, so the extension's release skill needs a changelog-writing step of its own. Until the first release the file is either empty or covers the unpublished `0.1.0` history, and that content depends on the release-notes-source and first-published-version questions.

The extension gets no file of its own. Its release entries go into the root `CHANGELOG.md` beside the plugin's, under a heading form that tells the two products apart, and the package carries that root file to both listings, through `vsce package`'s changelog-path option or a copy written into the package by `scripts/bundle.js`. The project keeps one changelog, so a reader of the repository finds every release of both products in one place, and no second file needs maintaining. The listings' changelog tabs would show the plugin's long release history, Cairn-era entries included, to readers who installed only the extension. `/release-plugin`'s heading count, its resume check, and its entry extraction all key on `## <VERSION> — ` headings in that file, so it would have to learn to skip extension entries, and an extension version could reuse a number the plugin already used (0.9.0 and later). The heading forms would also have to stay consistent with whatever tag and release forms the sibling questions settle.

The extension gets a changelog that is not tracked. Each package build writes it into the git-ignored build output, as `scripts/bundle.js` already writes `bundled/` from the checkout, composing it from the repository's record (for example the missions tool's finish summaries for `gurita-vscode/`, or the extension's release tags). The VSIX carries the generated file to both listings, and the root `CHANGELOG.md` is not changed. No changelog text is typed by hand or stored twice. The listings show the extension's own history, rebuilt from the same record every time, so it cannot drift from what was released. The package build would then depend on git history and on how the record is read, so a shallow clone or a build outside a checkout produces a wrong or empty changelog. The repository holds no readable changelog for the extension beside the VSIX. Whether this works depends on the release-notes-source and extension-release-tag questions, which decide what record there is to compose from.

The package carries a short tracked `gurita-vscode/CHANGELOG.md` that holds no entries, only a sentence sending the reader to where the extension's release notes are kept (for example the repository's GitHub releases), so both listings' changelog tabs show that pointer. The root `CHANGELOG.md` is not changed. The listings get a changelog tab that leads somewhere, and the file never needs editing at a release, so the release skill has no changelog step. A reader on a listing sees no change list and has to leave the listing to find one. It only works if release notes for the extension exist somewhere else, which depends on the extension-GitHub-release and release-notes-source questions. If they do not, the pointer leads nowhere.

The extension gets no changelog, now or until a later mission adds one. No file is created under `gurita-vscode/`, the package carries none, both listings show no changelog content, and the root `CHANGELOG.md` stays the plugin's alone. Whatever notes an extension release has are kept only wherever the sibling release questions put them, and the registries' own version lists. It adds no file, no release step, and no format to keep, and it leaves `/release-plugin` and the root changelog untouched. Because `vsce` picks up a `CHANGELOG.md` at the extension root whenever one appears, a changelog can be added at any later release without a change to the build. A listing reader cannot see what changed between versions, which public listings usually show and which matters once updates reach users automatically. How much this costs depends on whether the extension-GitHub-release and release-notes-source questions leave the notes anywhere at all.

open-question.question: A package bundles the missions tool, the fixed console lines, and the plugin version from the checkout it is built from. From which state of the repository may an extension release be built: any `main`, or only one whose bundled sources (`core/tools/missions.py`, `docs/skill-reference.md`, `VERSION`) are those of a released plugin version?
open-question.recommendation: `VERSION` moves only in a `Release:` commit, so a package built between plugin releases can bundle an unreleased missions tool and fixed lines under the last released number, which the harness check then reports as equal; a hard stop keeps every published package truthful about the plugin version it reports, and an extension-only change still ships whenever those three files are untouched.
open-question.alternative: An extension release may be built only from a `main` whose three bundled sources are byte-identical to those at the tag named by `VERSION`. The extension's own code may sit anywhere after that tag. The release skill checks this before it changes or publishes anything, and on a mismatch stops on a fixed line that names the differing files and the remedy: release the plugin first with `/release-plugin`, or wait. `scripts/bundle.js` and builds made by hand stay unrestricted. Every published package bundles exactly the missions tool and console lines of the plugin version it reports, so the harness check's version comparison is truthful, while extension-only changes still ship without waiting for a plugin release whenever `core/` and the reference are untouched. While `main` holds unreleased changes to the missions tool or the fixed-line table, no extension release is possible at all, an urgent extension fix included, until a plugin release is cut. The check also adds one more condition to the release skill and to its tests.

An extension release may be built from any `main`. The release skill makes no comparison between the bundled sources (`core/tools/missions.py`, `docs/skill-reference.md`, `VERSION`) and those of a plugin release, `scripts/bundle.js` stays as it is, and no rule about the bundled plugin state is written anywhere. Extension releases stay fully independent of the plugin's release cadence: an extension-only fix ships the moment it is ready, and nothing new is built, tested, or documented. `VERSION` changes only in a `Release:` commit, so between plugin releases `main` can carry a changed missions tool or fixed-line table under the last released version number. A package built then bundles an unreleased tool and console lines labelled as that release, the harness check reports the versions as equal, and a user running the released plugin meets the mismatch at run time with nothing pointing at it. It holds today only because `core/` and `docs/skill-reference.md` happen to be unchanged since `2.0.0`.

An extension release may be built from any `main`. Before it publishes, the release skill compares the three bundled sources with those at the tag named by `VERSION` (for example `git diff --quiet <VERSION> -- core/tools/missions.py docs/skill-reference.md VERSION`) and, if they differ, prints which ones differ. It then carries on and refuses nothing. The maintainer sees a mismatch before it goes public, but an extension release is never held back by unreleased plugin work, which may be harmless (a fixed line reworded, a missions-tool query the extension does not call). A warning does not stop a mismatched package. Whether anyone reads it depends on whether the skill pauses before publishing, which the sibling question on pre-publish confirmation decides, and a package that went out mismatched cannot be republished under the same version.

An extension release may be built from any `main`, but for a release build the three bundled sources are taken from the tag named by `VERSION` (through `git show <VERSION>:<path>`) rather than from the working tree. Either `scripts/bundle.js` gains a release mode or the release skill stages the files from the tag, and ordinary builds keep reading the checkout. A release is never blocked, and the package always carries a released plugin's tool and console lines that match the version it reports. The extension code on `main` may already rely on a newer missions-tool query or fixed line than the tag holds, so the published package can fail at run time in a way no local build or test showed. There are also two bundling paths, so the package the maintainer tested is not the one that ships.

An extension release may be built only from a commit that a plugin release tag points to, so the extension's own code and the bundled sources both come from a released plugin state. The release skill refuses any `HEAD` that does not carry the tag named by `VERSION`. The rule is the simplest to state and check, and the package, the plugin version, and the extension code all correspond to one released, tagged point in history. Every extension release is tied to a plugin release, so an extension-only change cannot ship until a plugin release is cut. That undoes the separate version of its own the extension was given, and it pushes extension releases into `/release-plugin`'s cadence and its tag lookup, which the sibling questions on extension tags and release notes are working to keep apart.

open-question.question: The goal has the first publication made through the new release skill, which only the maintainer runs. Is that run a task on the mission's list, or a step the maintainer takes after the task run and before finishing the mission, as the mission that first built the extension kept its install-and-try step off the list?
open-question.alternative: The first publication is carried on no task list at any time: `derive-tasks` authors no task for it, so `TASKS_TODO.md` holds only work leading up to it and the task run ends on its ordinary completion line. After the run the maintainer runs the new release skill by hand for the first version, the release's own commits being the only record of it, with no `Task-completion:` commit for the publication, and submits any follow-up the publication shows with `submit-task` while the mission is still live; the mission is finished only once the extension is live. This is the shape the first extension mission recorded for its install-and-try step. It follows the recorded precedent of the mission that built the extension, keeps the one irreversible public act (a version a registry accepted cannot be published again, a removed name cannot be reused) in the hands of the person who confirms it, and leaves no task on the list that an unattended completion run reaches and cannot carry out. The step the goal names as the mission's end stands on no list, so nothing in the workflow checks that it happened: `finish-mission`'s empty-list check passes before publication, and the mission treats its other maintainer-only steps (the publisher, the namespace, the tokens) as tasks while treating this one otherwise. Any task that needs the extension already live, such as one checking the listings, must be authored to come after it, by `submit-task` once it has run.

The first publication is the last task on the list, authored by `derive-tasks` after the tasks that build the release skill and the listing material, and completed as the mission's other maintainer-only tasks are completed: the maintainer runs the release skill, and the task is then closed with its own `Task-completion:` commit carrying its verified bar, the release's own commits landing separately. The list is the mission's whole path to the end state its goal fixes, so `finish-mission`'s empty-list check cannot pass before the extension is published, and the publication is handled the same way as the publisher, namespace, and token steps the goal already makes tasks, with its own recorded bar. An unattended completion run reaches a task its agent cannot carry out, and how such a task is completed and what it verifies depends on the axis the `Maintainer-only tasks` question owns; the publication's record is split between the release's commits and a separate task commit.

The first publication is the last task on the list and ordinary agent work: the completing agent runs the release skill itself, publishing the first version to both registries, and closes the task with its `Task-completion:` commit, the maintainer taking no step of their own for it beyond having put the tokens where the skill reads them. The whole mission, publication included, runs through to the extension being live in one unattended completion run, and the first real run of the release skill is itself the task that verifies it. It rejects the premise that only the maintainer runs the release skill and hands an irreversible public act to an unattended agent, so a mistake in the skill or the listing material is published with no person in the loop. It is viable only depending on the axes the `Publish site and tokens` question owns (whether the agent's run can reach the tokens or start the workflow) and the `Pre-publish confirmation` question owns (whether the skill stops for a confirmation no agent may give).

The list's last task is agent work rehearsing the release short of publishing: the agent carries the release skill's steps up to but not including any write to a registry (the package built, the skill's own checks passing) and records that as its bar. The publication itself is then the maintainer's step off the list, taken after the task run and before finishing, as in the off-the-list option, with follow-ups submitted through `submit-task`. A broken release skill or package is found inside the agent run, where fixing it costs a task, before the maintainer's one irreversible run, while that run stays with the maintainer. It adds a task and needs the release skill to have a way to stop before publishing, which it would carry only for this rehearsal, and the publication itself still stands on no list, with the off-the-list option's gap that nothing checks it happened before finish. A rehearsal reaching the token check depends on the axis the `Publish site and tokens` question owns.

open-question.question: The root `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, and `docs/` do not mention the extension, by a decision of the mission that first built it. Once it is published, does any of them gain a mention of it with links to its listings, and which?
open-question.recommendation: The reason the root documents stayed silent, an unpublished extension installed by hand, ends with the publication: the landing page is where a prospective user looks for how to install Gurita, and a contributor changing `gurita-vscode/` should learn from `CONTRIBUTING.md` that it has a build, test, and release path of its own, which only the context file records today.
open-question.alternative: After the first publication, the root `README.md` gains the short subsection with links to both listings and to `gurita-vscode/README.md`. `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s `## Development` gains a pointer: the extension under `gurita-vscode/` has a build and test loop of its own (Node 22 through nvm, independent of the host build and `VERSION`), documented in its README, and is released through its own maintainer-only skill rather than `/release-plugin`. `docs/` stays untouched. Covers both audiences the extension now has: users find it on the landing page, and contributors learn that a change under `gurita-vscode/` follows a different build, test, and release path. Today only `CLAUDE.md` records that path. Adds contributor prose that has to follow the extension's tooling and release skill as they change. Its wording depends on how the sibling questions on the release skill and on CI for the extension settle.

Keep the first extension mission's decision as it stands: the root `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, and `docs/` stay untouched by this mission, the two listings and `gurita-vscode/README.md` stay the extension's only documentation, and the root documents are left for a later mission to change, if any ever does. Costs nothing and reopens no recorded decision. The root documents stay about the plugin alone, the extension's documentation keeps one home, and a reader on a listing still reaches the repository through the manifest's `repository` entry. A reader who arrives at the plugin's repository or reads its docs never learns that a published extension exists. The only path to it is a registry search, so the publication this mission is for stays almost invisible from the project's own landing page.

After the first publication, the root `README.md` gains a short prose subsection, for example `### VS Code extension` under `## Installation` beside the three host subsections. In one or two sentences it says what the extension is, links to its Marketplace and Open VSX listings, and links to `gurita-vscode/README.md` for its use documentation. `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `docs/` stay untouched. Puts the extension where a prospective user already looks for how to install Gurita, at the cost of a few lines in one file. Everything else about it stays in the extension's own README. Partly reverses the earlier one-README decision. The root README now carries listing URLs that must stay correct if the extension's identifier or listings ever change, and a contributor reading `CONTRIBUTING.md` still finds no word of the extension's separate build and release path.

After the first publication, the root `README.md`'s centred badge row gains a Marketplace badge and an Open VSX badge, each showing the published version or install count and linking to its listing. No prose is added anywhere, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `docs/` stay untouched. The smallest visible mention, in a form the README already uses for its release, CI, and license badges. It changes no section of the README's text and shows at a glance that the extension is live and which version is. A badge says nothing about what the extension does or how it relates to the plugin, so a reader has to click through to learn it. It also depends on a third-party badge service still supporting both registries, a dependency the README's existing GitHub-based badges do not have.

After the first publication, the root `README.md` gains the short subsection with links to both listings and to `gurita-vscode/README.md`. `docs/ways-of-using.md` also gains a brief mention that the extension runs these headless chains as recipes from a VS Code side bar, with the same links. `CONTRIBUTING.md` stays untouched. Reaches the reader at the point where the extension is most useful: the ways-of-using page describes the chains it runs, so a reader typing those lines by hand learns that a published tool runs them. Spreads listing links across two user-facing documents that must be kept in step. The ways-of-using page, so far purely about command lines, gains a pointer to a separate product whose recipe file (`gurita-vscode/shipped_recipes.md`) can drift from the page's chains.

After the first publication, all three gain a mention: the root `README.md` gets the short subsection with links to both listings and to `gurita-vscode/README.md`, `docs/ways-of-using.md` gets the brief mention that the extension runs the chains as recipes, with the same links, and `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s `## Development` gets the pointer to the extension's own build, test, and release path. Fully reverses the earlier decision now that the reason for it, an unpublished, hand-installed extension, no longer holds. Every root document a user or contributor reads acknowledges the extension where it bears. The largest edit and the most surfaces to keep correct: listing links in two documents and contributor prose in a third. Some of the extension's description is repeated outside its own README, which the one-README decision existed to prevent.

After the first publication, the root `README.md` gains the short subsection with links to both listings and to `gurita-vscode/README.md`. The same subsection is added to each host's README template under `scripts/hosts/<host>/`, so the published distribution repositories carry it too once the next plugin release publishes them. `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `docs/` stay untouched. Reaches the readers most likely to want the extension: people who install the plugin from a distribution repository and may never open the root repository. Goes beyond the three root documents the question names. It requires a host rebuild under the drift gate, it shows in the distribution repositories only after a plugin release, and it puts the same listing links in four READMEs.

open-question.question: The goal makes creating the Marketplace publisher and the Open VSX namespace and issuing the two tokens the mission's first tasks, but a task run is carried out by an agent that can do none of them. What does completing such a task consist of: who does what, and what does the task verify before it counts as done?
open-question.alternative: The account steps stay tasks on the list, and the maintainer takes them by hand before the task run, as in the gate task with a token check. The task the runner completes is verification only, but the check stops short of the tokens' validity. The bar holds that the publisher and the namespace exist, observed through a public registry query with no token, and that each token is present under the name the release skill will read, by name only, for example a variable set in the maintainer's shell or a secret listed by `gh secret list`. No token value ever passes through the runner. When a check fails the agent returns `FAILED:` naming what is missing, and the run stops before any later task. It checks what can be checked wherever the tokens are kept, with no secret ever read by an agent or written into its transcript, and it still stops the run until the accounts exist. A token that is present but expired, mis-scoped, or issued for another publisher passes the task and fails only at the first publication. What "present by name" means depends on where the tokens are kept, an axis the "Publish site and tokens" question owns.

The account steps stay tasks on the list. The maintainer takes them by hand before the task run starts: creating the Marketplace publisher `uhappylogic` on the web, creating an Eclipse account and signing the Open VSX publisher agreement, and issuing both tokens. The task the runner then completes, the agent's or the inline one alike, is verification only, with whatever can be scripted once the token exists done by the runner. Creating the Open VSX namespace through `ovsx create-namespace` is one such step. The bar holds three checks: the publisher and the namespace exist, observed through a registry query; each token is accepted by its registry for `uhappylogic`, through `vsce verify-pat` and `ovsx verify-pat`; and the token stands where the release skill will read it. When a check fails the agent returns `FAILED:` with what the maintainer must still do, the run stops before any later task, and a re-run once the steps are taken completes the task. The commit records the bar and the task list's removal only. The task counts as done only when the registries themselves accept what the first publication will use. A wrong publisher ID, a token issued with the wrong scope, or a token in the wrong place is caught at the mission's first task, not at the release run at its end. The runner must be able to read the token to verify it, so the bar depends on where the tokens are kept, an axis the "Publish site and tokens" question owns: a token held only as an Actions secret cannot be checked by a local agent. Every unattended run also stops on this task until the maintainer has acted, and `ovsx` must be fetched for the run, since it is installed nowhere.

alternative.id: Inline task, maintainer in the loop

open-question.alternative: The account steps stay tasks on the list, completed only through the inline `/complete-task` in a conversation with the maintainer, never by the dispatched agent. The runner states the exact steps: the publisher and namespace IDs, the token scopes, and where each token goes. The maintainer takes them in the browser and says when each is done. The runner then checks what it can reach, the publisher and the namespace through a registry query and each token through its registry's verify command where it can read it. It derives the bar from those checks and commits. A `/complete-all-tasks` run reaching such a task while it stands returns `FAILED:`, so the maintainer completes these tasks inline before handing the rest of the list to an unattended run. The guidance and the verification happen in the one session where the maintainer acts, so a step taken wrongly is caught and redone at once rather than on a re-run, and the task's commit still carries a checked bar. These tasks can never be completed unattended, which breaks the uniform run every other task of the list gets: a `/complete-all-tasks` started first stops at once. How much the runner can verify still depends on where the tokens are kept, an axis the "Publish site and tokens" question owns.

The account steps stay tasks on the list, completed through the inline `/complete-task` with the maintainer. The maintainer takes the steps and confirms them, and the task counts as done on that confirmation alone, with nothing queried against either registry and no token checked. The bar records the maintainer's statements, for example that the publisher `uhappylogic` exists and that both tokens are issued and stored. The dispatched agent, holding no maintainer to ask, returns `FAILED:` on such a task. It is the simplest completion and needs no registry query, no `ovsx` install, and no token access by the runner, whatever the "Publish site and tokens" question settles. The recorded bar is a claim, not an observation, so a mistyped publisher ID or a bad token surfaces only when the release skill first publishes, at the mission's end. These tasks also cannot be completed unattended.

The account steps stay tasks on the list, but what each task delivers is the written procedure for them, a work product an agent can produce: how to create the publisher and the namespace, which scopes each token takes, how long it lives, where it is stored, and how to rotate it. open-question.question: The pinned vsce refuses an SVG file as the manifest's icon, and the repository tracks no raster image and no script that writes one. open-question.recommendation: It repeats the pattern the repository's other two images follow, a tracked drawing, a stdlib generator, a committed output, and a drift test that both pytest runs and CI already execute, and filled outlines on a flat tile need only a small scanline fill and a `zlib` PNG writer, with no new dependency.

The repository gains its own rasterizer, a few hundred lines of fill, anti-aliasing, and PNG encoding that `render_icon.py`'s outline code does not give for free, and byte equality can depend on the `zlib` build, so the test may need to compare decoded pixels; it only fits if the design the sibling question settles is expressible from the repository's text drawings rather than as free-hand art.

The same stdlib-only Python rasterizer is run during packaging, from `vscode:prepublish` (through `scripts/bundle.js` or a script beside it), writing the PNG into a git-ignored location the package carries, as `bundled/` is written today; no raster file is committed, and no drift test is needed because the file is always derived fresh from the tracked drawings. alternative.id: Pinned npm converter at package time

open-question.alternative: A tracked SVG of the listing icon (generated by a stdlib script as the activity-bar SVG is, or kept as a source file) is converted to PNG during `vscode:prepublish` by a pinned npm dev dependency that renders SVG (such as `@resvg/resvg-js`), recorded in `package-lock.json`; the PNG is written to a git-ignored location the package carries and nothing raster is committed. A tracked SVG of the listing icon is converted to PNG by a tracked script using a pinned npm dev dependency that renders SVG, run by hand after a drawing changes; the PNG is committed and named by the manifest's `icon`, and a `node:test` test re-renders the SVG and compares it with the committed file. The committed icon is reviewable in its commit and checked against its source by a test, without the repository writing its own rasterizer. alternative.id: Local system tool at package time

open-question.alternative: A tracked SVG of the listing icon is converted to PNG during packaging by a command-line tool installed on the packaging machine (ImageMagick's `magick`, present here, or macOS `sips`), invoked from the package scripts; the PNG is git-ignored and nothing raster is committed, and no dependency is added to the project. Packaging then depends on a tool outside the project that a fresh checkout, CI, or another contributor may lack (`sips` exists only on macOS) and whose output varies by version; it holds only while the release is built on the maintainer's machine, a condition on the sibling question of where the release skill publishes from.

Nothing ties the committed PNG to its source, so a changed SVG left unconverted ships a stale icon with no check failing, breaking the generated-and-tested convention the repository's other two images follow, and the result depends on the converter's version on the day it was run.

The listing icon is drawn or exported directly as a PNG in an image editor and committed under `gurita-vscode/media/` as its own source, with no SVG or text drawing behind it and no generator; at most a test checks that it is a well-formed PNG of the listing size. It suits a design that is free-hand art rather than something the text drawings can express, and it leaves no source and derived file that could disagree. The icon cannot be regenerated from the repository's drawings, so it drifts from the activity-bar icon and banner whenever they change, and any edit needs an image editor and produces an opaque binary diff; it is viable only if the design the sibling question settles is not drawn from the existing drawings.

The README the listings show is a short introduction only: what the extension is and that it drives the Gurita plugin rather than replacing it, what it needs (the plugin installed in the harnesses it drives, `python3`, the supported platforms), a few sentences on what it shows (live missions in a side bar, a window per mission, recipes run in a terminal, a looped task run), and a link to the full use documentation in the repository, with no section per feature. The listing text is small and changes rarely, so a release almost never has to touch it, and the extension's whole use documentation keeps exactly one home that is maintained as it is today. Neither the listing nor the editor's installed-extension details page tells a user how to do anything, so every first use sends them to the repository, whose current text may document a version other than the one installed unless the link is pinned to a release ref, which depends on the sibling question on the extension release tag; where that full documentation stands depends on the sibling question on the listing README file.

open-question.question: Does an extension release make a commit of its own, and under which subject, given that `/release-plugin` recognises its own interrupted run by a `HEAD` subject of exactly `Release: <VERSION>`?
open-question.alternative: The release skill makes one commit of its own, holding only what the release writes into the tree (the extension's version slots and any changelog entry), under a new marker that does not open with `Release:`, `Extension-release: <VERSION>` with the version as the whole descriptor. The release skill makes one commit of its own under the plugin's exact form, `Release: <VERSION>` with the extension's version, and `/release-plugin`'s resumption detection is changed so that a matching subject counts only when that commit also changed the root `VERSION` (or another plugin-only file) to `<VERSION>`; the extension skill applies the mirror test on `gurita-vscode/package.json`. One uniform release subject for the whole repository, with each skill's resumption test keyed on what the commit actually changed rather than on its wording alone. It edits `/release-plugin`, a working release path, to defend against a collision another choice would never create, and the subject alone no longer says which artifact a release commit released, so a plugin and an extension release of the same version number produce identical subjects in the log.

open-question.question: Does an extension release create a GitHub release in `uHappyLogic/gurita`, with or without the VSIX attached, or do the two registries alone carry it?

open-question.question: Which conditions must hold before the extension's release skill changes or publishes anything, for example a clean tracked tree, `main` not behind `origin/main`, the extension's tests and the runner's tests passing, a package that builds, and tokens both registries still accept?

alternative.id: Full gate with live token check

open-question.alternative: Before it writes or publishes anything, the skill runs a fixed set of hard stops, each ending the run with nothing changed and the reason reported, never waived. Repository state: the tracked tree is clean, `HEAD` is on `main`, `main` is not behind `origin/main` after a fetch, and no untracked file stands under the extension's source paths outside its git-ignored build directories. Toolchain: Node 22 answers through nvm, `npm ci` installs the pinned dependencies, and `vsce` and the Open VSX publishing tool both resolve. Tests: the extension's `node:test` suite (`npm test`) and the runner's `runner_tests/` pass. Build: `npm run package` builds the VSIX into the ignored `dist/`. Tokens: each registry's token is checked live against that registry for the `uhappylogic` publisher or namespace (the verify-token commands both publishing tools offer), which also confirms the publisher and the namespace exist. Every failure a publish could meet, a stale or dirty tree, a broken build, failing tests, and an expired, wrongly scoped, or missing token or publisher, is caught before either registry is touched, so a release can no longer stop with one registry holding the version and the other not because of anything checkable in advance; it carries `/release-plugin`'s gate-before-write rule over to the extension. The slowest and most involved pre-flight: it needs network access to both registries and sends both tokens before publishing, adds the Open VSX publishing tool as something the run must find, and its token step's form depends on where the tokens are kept and where the skill runs, an axis the publish-site question owns; on a workflow run the clean-tree and behind-origin checks become largely moot.

The same repository-state, toolchain, test, and build stops as the full gate, all hard stops, but the tokens are checked only for being present and readable where the skill reads them (set and non-empty), with no query to either registry before publishing. Catches the common misconfiguration, a token never set or not visible to the run, without any network call to the registries or any use of a token before the publish itself, and needs no verify command from either publishing tool. An expired, revoked, or wrongly scoped token, or a publisher or namespace that does not exist, surfaces only at publish time, possibly after the first registry already accepted the version, which leaves exactly the half-published state a sibling question has to handle; where the tokens live, and so what "present" means, is owned by the publish-site question.

alternative.id: Full gate plus whole suite and package inspection

open-question.alternative: Everything the full gate with live token check runs, and two further hard stops: the repository's whole Python suite at both interpreters (`uv run pytest` and the 3.9 floor run), which also covers the missions tool the package bundles, and an inspection of the built VSIX's file list and manifest, stopping when it holds anything under `mission_*`, sources, or tests, or lacks the listing icon, the listing README, the license, or the bundled files. Also guards what the package carries rather than only that it builds: a `.vscodeignore` slip shipping mission files or sources, or a listing asset missing from the package, is stopped before it becomes a public, unremovable version, and the bundled missions tool is tested in the same run. The longest run, repeating checks the plugin's own release and CI already make, and the content inspection is a second list of expected files that must be kept in step with `.vscodeignore` and the listing assets by hand; whether the bundled sources must be those of a released plugin version is a separate question this inspection does not settle.

The skill stops before writing anything only on repository state (clean tracked tree, `HEAD` on `main`, not behind `origin/main`, no untracked file under the extension's sources) and on a live check of both registries' tokens; it runs no tests and makes no package build in the pre-flight, the package being built only by the publish step itself. A short, fast pre-flight that still blocks the two failures most likely to produce an unreproducible or half-published release, while relying on every task of the missions that changed the extension having already verified its tests and build before its commit. A failing test or a broken package from a hand commit or a dependency drift is found only when the publish step builds, or not at all when the build succeeds but the code is wrong, and a published version cannot be republished; the token step's form again depends on the publish-site question.

The skill has no gate of its own: it builds and publishes directly, and a failure of the build, a publishing tool, or a registry stops it with that tool's own message; the conditions the question lists are left to the maintainer to see to before invoking it. The simplest skill to write and keep: nothing duplicates what the publishing tools already refuse, and the run is as short as publishing allows. Nothing stops a release from a dirty, outdated, or wrong-branch tree, a failing test suite ships, and a token or publisher problem on the second registry is found only after the first accepted the version, leaving a half-published release; it also breaks with `/release-plugin`'s rule that every gate passes before anything is changed or published.

open-question.question: From what are the notes of an extension release composed: the finish summaries of the missions scoped to `gurita-vscode/` since the previous extension release, as `/release-plugin` composes the plugin's notes from finished missions, the commits in between, or text the maintainer writes?
open-question.alternative: The notes are composed by the release skill from the finish summaries of the missions whose directory lies under `gurita-vscode/` and that were finished since the previous extension release, read through `missions.py missions` and `summary` and rewritten into one condensed `###` section per mission, newest finish first, exactly as `/release-plugin`'s step 5 does. It reuses a composition the project already runs and trusts, from a record every extension mission already writes through `/finish-mission`, so the notes cost nothing extra to produce, match the plugin's release-note shape, and a version-only rebuild still has a path that never takes itself silently. The notes are composed from finish summaries as in the first option, but the mission set is every mission finished since the previous extension release that changed what the package carries, whatever its scope: the missions under `gurita-vscode/` and also root-scoped plugin missions that changed a bundled source (`core/tools/missions.py`, `docs/skill-reference.md`, `VERSION`) or a path under `gurita-vscode/`. How far plugin changes reach a package also depends on the sibling deciding from which repository state a release may be built.

The notes are composed from the commits between the previous extension release and `HEAD` that changed a path under `gurita-vscode/` or a bundled source, their subjects and, where a subject is not self-explanatory, their bodies, condensed into one bulleted section of user-facing changes. Mission summaries are not read and the maintainer writes no text. It needs no finished mission, so it reports everything the package actually received, the publishing mission's own unfinished work and hand commits included, and it works the same on the first release as on every later one. The range's start depends on the sibling owning the extension's release marker.

The notes are text the maintainer writes for each release, given to the skill as its input or typed when the skill asks for it, and published verbatim; the skill composes nothing from missions or commits. The maintainer says exactly what a listing reader should know, including changes no mission summary or commit subject names well, and the skill carries no composition logic to write, test, or keep in step with `/release-plugin`'s. Every release costs the maintainer writing and recalling what changed, with nothing checking the text against what was released, and the skill can never run unattended, which constrains the sibling deciding whether it pauses for confirmation.

The skill composes a draft from the finish summaries of the missions under `gurita-vscode/` finished since the previous extension release, falling back to the commit range on an empty range, and the maintainer then revises or adds to it, for instance to name the work of a mission still live at release time, before the text is used; the maintainer's revised text is what is published. The routine case costs the maintainer only a review, while work the finished-mission record cannot show, the publishing mission's own listing work on the first release above all, can still be stated in the notes. The notes are no longer reproducible from the record, two runs can publish different text for one version, and the revision step needs a point in the run where the maintainer is present, which depends on the sibling deciding whether the skill pauses before publishing.

An extension release carries no notes of its own: nothing is composed or written, and the listings show the version and the README alone, the record of what changed staying in the repository's mission and commit history. The skill has no composition step at all, and no text exists that can drift from the history or differ between the two registries. A user updating from a listing has no way to see what a version changed without reading the repository's history. It is coherent only if the release writes notes nowhere, which depends on the siblings deciding whether the extension gets a changelog and whether a release creates a GitHub release.

open-question.question: A version a registry has accepted cannot be published to it again. What does a re-run of the extension's release skill with the same version do after one of the two registries accepted that version and the other did not?
open-question.alternative: Before each publish, the re-run asks the registry whether it already holds the version (the Marketplace through `vsce show`, Open VSX through its public REST query on `uhappylogic/gurita-vscode/<version>`). It skips the registry that does and publishes only to the one that does not, from a package rebuilt from the state the version was released from, then goes on to whatever later release steps remain. This is the check-then-do resumption `/release-plugin` already uses for each of its publish steps. A re-run with the same version finishes the release exactly where it stopped, with one rule, query first and skip when done, shared with the plugin's release skill, and the skill can tell the maintainer which registry it skipped and which it published to. It needs a query per registry written into the skill and depends on each registry's read side reporting a version soon after the version is accepted. The rebuilt package matches the one already accepted only if the rebuild starts from the same repository state, which leans on how the release records that state (the sibling questions on the release commit and the tag).

The re-run asks no registry anything. It runs both publishes again, each with the `--skip-duplicate` flag that the pinned `vsce` 4.1.1 offers ("Fail silently if version already exists on the marketplace") and that `ovsx publish` also offers. The registry that already holds the version turns its publish into a silent success, and the other one receives the version from a package rebuilt from the state the version was released from. Of all the ways to resume, this one adds the least to the skill: the same two publish commands serve the first run and every re-run, with no query code and no branch. The skill cannot tell a duplicate it skipped from a fresh publish, so its report cannot say which registry the re-run actually published to. It also relies on both CLIs keeping the flag's behaviour across upgrades, and a skipped duplicate is never checked against the package that was accepted.

As in the query-and-resume option, the re-run queries each registry and publishes only to the one missing the version. What it publishes is not a rebuild but the very VSIX file the first run built and published to the registry that accepted it. That file is kept where the re-run can find it under the version's name, for example under `dist/` on the publishing machine or as a release asset. Both registries are guaranteed to carry the same bytes for the version, whatever happened to the checkout, its bundled sources, or the toolchain between the two runs. The release has to keep a built artifact the repository has so far never kept (`dist/` is git-ignored and the VSIX is never committed), and a re-run whose retained file is gone has nothing to publish. Whether a file survives between runs depends on the sibling question of where the release publishes from, since a workflow run's workspace does not outlive it.

The re-run queries both registries. When exactly one holds the version, it publishes nothing and stops, printing which registry is missing the version and the exact `vsce publish` or `ovsx publish` command the maintainer runs on the package to finish. This follows the way `/release-plugin` prints the commands for a missing repository or token and exits without running them. The skill never publishes in a state it did not start from cleanly, so the irreversible second publish is a deliberate act by the maintainer, and the skill needs no resume path past the publish steps. A transient failure, such as a network error or a registry outage, costs the maintainer a hand step outside the skill, done with a CLI and a token they must have at hand. Any release steps that follow the publishes are left for the maintainer to finish by hand or by a further re-run.

The skill has no logic for a half-published version. A re-run with the same version runs its steps as on a first run, the registry that already holds the version refuses the publish, and the skill stops on that registry's error. Completing the release on the other registry is left wholly to the maintainer, who publishes by hand. Nothing is added to the skill for a case that may never arise once its pre-flight checks pass, and the registry's own refusal keeps the accepted version from being overwritten. The one failure the question names ends in a stop with no guidance. A re-run, the natural response, can never succeed for that version, so the maintainer has to work out the missing publish alone. How often this happens depends on the sibling question of which pre-flight checks run first (tokens both registries still accept among them).

Once either registry holds a version, a re-run with that version refuses, naming the registry that holds it. The release is completed by running the skill with the next version, which goes to both registries, and the half-published version stays on the one registry that accepted it. No version is ever published in two separate runs, so the two registries never carry bytes for one version that were built at different times, and the skill needs only one "version already taken" check. The registries' version histories diverge for good, with a version that exists on only one of them. Every half-published attempt also burns a version number and repeats the whole release, version write, notes, and any commit or tag included. How much of that repeats depends on the sibling questions of where the version comes from and whether the release commits and tags.

open-question.question: CI sets up no Node, so neither the extension's `node:test` tests nor a package build runs there. Does this mission add them to CI now that the extension is published, or do they stay checked only where the maintainer runs them?

recommendation.option: Tests and package in the drift-gate job

open-question.recommendation: A published package bundles `core/tools/missions.py`, the fixed-line table, and `VERSION`, so a plugin-side push can break it, and building it on every push means a release is never the first place that shows; it stays one job with no path filter, as the drift gate is documented to be, and the pinned `vsce` cannot change its rules under it.

alternative.id: Tests and package in the drift-gate job

open-question.alternative: The existing `drift-gate` job gains a Node setup (`actions/setup-node`, pinned to a SHA, Node 22), `npm ci`, `npm test`, and `npm run package` in `gurita-vscode/`. That last step runs `vscode:prepublish`, which compiles, runs `scripts/bundle.js` from the checkout, and calls `vsce package`. The built VSIX is discarded, and there is still one job and no path filter. Every push proves that the published artifact still builds: the compile, the tests, the bundling of `missions.py`, the fixed lines, and `VERSION`, and `vsce`'s acceptance of the manifest, icon, and README. A release is then never the first place a broken package shows, and all of this is reported under the one existing status. The heaviest change to the one job: every push, plugin-only ones included, pays for Node, `npm ci`, and a `vsce` run, and a `vsce` validation rule that changes upstream can turn the plugin's drift gate red. If the icon is written at package time, CI must also be able to produce it, which depends on how the listing icon is produced, an axis a sibling question owns.

CI stays as it is: `drift-gate.yml` keeps setting up no Node, and the extension's `node:test` tests and its package build are run only by the maintainer, by hand or from the extension's release skill. The mission adds no workflow and no step, and the question is left for a later mission to take up if a broken push ever shows the need. Costs nothing and adds no pinned action to bump by hand. The extension has one maintainer, its tests already run locally under nvm's Node 22, and CI's single job stays exactly the drift gate and the two pytest runs it is documented to be. A push or merged pull request that breaks the extension's compile, its tests, or the package, including a change under `core/tools/missions.py`, `docs/skill-reference.md`, or `VERSION` that `scripts/bundle.js` bundles, passes CI green and shows up only when the maintainer next builds or releases. Whether a release catches it depends on the release pre-flight checks, which a sibling question owns.

The existing `drift-gate` job gains a Node setup (`actions/setup-node`, pinned to a SHA, Node 22 to match the version nvm provides locally) followed by `npm ci` and `npm test` in `gurita-vscode/`. There is still one job and no path filter, and no package build runs in CI. One status covers the plugin and the extension, as CONTRIBUTING.md describes for the drift gate. Every push compiles the TypeScript and runs the `node:test` suite at a small cost, and no separate workflow has to be kept in step. Nothing in CI checks that `vsce` still accepts the package, for example the manifest's icon or the README's images, or that `scripts/bundle.js` still finds its inputs, so a package-level break still surfaces only at release. Every plugin-only push also pays for the Node setup and `npm ci`, and there is one more pinned action to bump by hand.

A new workflow file beside `drift-gate.yml`, for the extension alone, with its own job: a Node setup pinned to a SHA (Node 22), `npm ci`, and `npm test` in `gurita-vscode/`. It runs on push and pull request, path-filtered to `gurita-vscode/**` and the files it builds from. `drift-gate.yml` is left unchanged and no package build runs. The drift gate keeps its documented one-job shape, and plugin-only pushes pay nothing for Node. An extension failure shows as its own status, separate from the plugin's gate. The path filter is a hand-maintained copy of the extension's input set, the same objection CLAUDE.md records against a `paths` list on the drift gate, so a missed input lets a breaking change through unchecked. There are two workflows and two statuses to keep, and nothing checks that the package still builds.

A new workflow file beside `drift-gate.yml`, for the extension alone, with its own job: a Node setup pinned to a SHA (Node 22), `npm ci`, `npm test`, and `npm run package` in `gurita-vscode/`, with the VSIX discarded. It runs on push and pull request, path-filtered to `gurita-vscode/**` and the sources `scripts/bundle.js` and the package read (`core/tools/missions.py`, `docs/skill-reference.md`, `VERSION`, the root `LICENSE`). `drift-gate.yml` is left unchanged. Covers the whole published artifact, as the in-job variant does, while keeping the drift gate's one-job shape and sparing plugin-only pushes the Node and `vsce` cost. A failure is reported as the extension's own status. The path filter has to track the bundle's inputs by hand and silently stops covering one it misses, the objection CLAUDE.md records against a filtered drift gate. It adds a second workflow and status to maintain, and like the in-job variant it depends on CI being able to produce the listing icon if that is written at package time, an axis a sibling question owns.

open-question.question: `/release-plugin` composes the plugin's release notes from every mission finished since the last tag, whatever its scope, so the next plugin release would list the missions scoped to `gurita-vscode/`. Do those missions stay in the plugin's release notes, or does `/release-plugin` leave them out once the extension has releases of its own?
open-question.alternative: `/release-plugin`'s step 5 drops every finished mission whose path lies under `gurita-vscode/`, from the next plugin release on, the three extension missions already finished after `2.0.0` included; a mission scoped elsewhere, the root included, stays in the plugin's notes even when it changed the extension. The test is the path field `missions .` already prints, so no new query is needed. The plugin's notes describe only what the plugin's users receive, through a one-line, mechanical filter on a field the skill already reads, with no cutoff date or tag to track. The three missions finished before the extension has a release of its own appear in no plugin notes, so they are recorded publicly only if the extension's notes take them up, which turns on how the sibling question on the release notes source settles; a root-scoped mission that changes only the extension still lands in the plugin's notes.

`/release-plugin` stays as it is: step 5 keeps every mission `missions.py missions .` lists as finished since the last tag, whatever its scope, so the three extension missions already finished after `2.0.0` and every later mission scoped to `gurita-vscode/` get full sections in the plugin's `CHANGELOG.md` entry and GitHub release, beside the extension's own release notes. This mission changes nothing in the skill, and a later mission may still split the notes. Nothing in `/release-plugin` changes, and the root changelog stays the one complete record of everything finished in the repository, so no mission's record depends on how the extension's own notes are composed. Plugin users, who install from the `gurita-<host>` distribution repositories that carry no extension, read sections about changes their release does not contain, and each extension mission's summary is published twice, once in each product's notes.

`/release-plugin`'s step 5 drops a finished mission whose path lies under `gurita-vscode/` only when it was finished after the extension's first release, so the three extension missions already finished after `2.0.0`, and any finished before that first release, stay as full sections in the next plugin release's notes, and later ones are left to the extension's own notes. Every extension mission gets exactly one public record: those predating the extension's releases in the plugin's notes, the rest in the extension's, with none dropped and none duplicated. The skill needs a cutoff it can read, the extension's first release, which exists only in whatever form the sibling questions on the extension's tag and release commit give it, and the rule keeps a one-off transition branch in `/release-plugin` for good.

`/release-plugin`'s step 5 drops a finished mission whenever every file its task commits changed lies under `gurita-vscode/`, whatever its scope, and keeps any mission that changed a file outside it, the plugin's `core/`, tools, or docs among them; it applies from the next plugin release on, the three already finished extension missions included. The rule follows what each mission actually changed rather than where it was placed, so a root-scoped mission that touched only the extension leaves the plugin's notes and an extension mission that also changed a plugin file stays in them. The skill must read each kept mission's task commits and their file lists, which `missions` and `summary` do not print, adding per-mission history reads and a judgment on mixed missions to a release step that today reads two queries; the three already finished missions' public record depends on the extension's notes source as under the scope rule.

`/release-plugin` keeps every finished mission, but step 5 composes the missions whose path lies under `gurita-vscode/` into one section of their own at the end of the plugin's entry, headed as the VS Code extension's, apart from the plugin's per-mission sections, in full as today. No mission's record is lost whatever the extension's own notes become, while a plugin user can see at a glance which changes are not part of the plugin. The extension's changes are still published in the plugin's changelog and GitHub release and again in the extension's notes, and the skill gains a grouping rule and a second section shape to keep.

`/release-plugin` composes no section for a mission whose path lies under `gurita-vscode/`; in their place the plugin's entry carries one line naming those missions' titles and pointing at where the extension's own notes stand. Plugin readers keep a trace that the extension changed in the same interval without reading its detail, and the detail is published once, in the extension's notes. The line needs a stable target to point at, which exists only if the sibling questions on the extension's changelog and GitHub release give it one, and the three missions already finished are reduced to titles if the extension's notes do not take them up.

open-question.question: Does the extension's release skill pause for the maintainer's confirmation before it publishes, as `/release-plugin` pauses once before anything public, or run through unattended once its checks pass?
open-question.alternative: The skill pauses exactly once, on every run, after its pre-flight checks and all local work and before anything public (the first registry upload, and any push, tag, or GitHub release the release makes). The pause shows the version about to be published and the release notes in full, verbatim, as they will be published. It accepts three answers, as `/release-plugin`'s step 7 does: an explicit publish proceeds, a stated revision of the notes is applied and the version and notes are shown again, and anything else stops with nothing public done. The gate is never skipped and no flag bypasses it. It mirrors the one pause `/release-plugin` already has and its maintainer already knows, placed at the one point where everything before is undoable and everything after is permanent (a version a registry has accepted cannot be published to it again), so the maintainer vetoes or fixes the public text before it is out. The run cannot complete unattended or in a headless chain. What the pause shows, and whether a revision can be applied in place, depends on whether the release composes notes and records them in a commit of its own, axes the Release notes source, Extension changelog, and Release commit subject questions own.

alternative.id: Single pause on the built package

open-question.alternative: The skill pauses exactly once, on every run, after the VSIX has been built and before anything public. The pause shows the version, the release notes where the release has any, and the built package itself: its path, size, and file list, which is what both listings will show (the README, the icon, the manifest's listing metadata). It invites the maintainer to install that VSIX into VS Code by hand (`code --install-extension` on its path) and try it before answering. An explicit publish proceeds and anything else stops with nothing public done. The gate is never skipped and no flag bypasses it. It catches a defect in the package itself, such as a README that renders wrongly, a missing bundled file, or a wrong icon, on the exact artifact the registries will receive and before either can accept a version that can never be published again. It is the longest pause, adding a hand install and a try to every release, including routine ones where the package changed little, and the file list it shows is long (37 files today) for a maintainer to read on each run.

The skill pauses twice on every run: once before it publishes to the first registry, showing the version and the notes, and once more after the first registry has accepted the version and before it publishes to the second, inviting the maintainer to look at the first listing as it now stands. An explicit publish at each pause proceeds; anything else stops, the second time with one registry carrying the version and the other not. Neither pause is skipped. A defect that shows only on a live listing (how the README, icon, or metadata render on the registry's page) stops the release before it reaches the second registry. It doubles the prompts, and a stop at the second pause leaves a half-published release by the maintainer's own choice, a state whose re-run behaviour the Half-published release question owns, while the first registry's version stays published and unrepairable anyway.

The skill pauses once, before anything public, showing the version and the notes, only when the extension is not yet listed on the registries, which it learns by querying them; once the extension is live on both, every later release runs through unattended once its pre-flight checks pass. No flag changes either behaviour. It puts the human check where the novelty is, the first appearance of the publisher, the listing name, and its metadata, which cannot be renamed or reused once wrong, while routine releases afterwards need no attendance. Every later release publishes a version and notes that no one reviewed before they became permanent, and the skill gains a registry query and a branch on its result, a second behaviour to maintain for what is a single run (the mission's own first publication).

The skill pauses once by default, before anything public, showing the version and the notes, with explicit publish proceeding and anything else stopping. A flag given on the invocation (for example `--yes`) skips the pause, so the run goes through unattended once its pre-flight checks pass. The maintainer reviews by default, yet a scripted or headless release is possible without editing the skill. It adds a second mode to a maintainer-only skill run by one person, and departs from `/release-plugin`, whose pause is never skipped; a flag habitually given turns the gate into no gate, with an irreversible publication behind it.

The skill never pauses: the maintainer's invocation is the consent, and once its pre-flight checks pass it publishes to both registries unattended. Whatever it shows of the version and the notes it prints as it goes, after the fact. It is the simplest skill and the fastest run, it completes in a headless chain with nothing to answer, and the version to release is already stated by the maintainer at invocation wherever the skill takes it as an argument. Nothing the run composes or builds, notes, listing text, or package, is seen before it becomes permanent on two registries that never accept the same version twice, so a mistake costs a new version to correct. How much the invocation already says depends on whether the version is given as an argument, an axis the Version source at release question owns.

The skill itself never pauses: it starts the publishing workflow once its checks pass, and the workflow's publish job runs under a GitHub Actions environment with the maintainer as its required reviewer, so publication waits until the maintainer approves the job on GitHub, where the run's version and inputs are shown; a rejected or unapproved job publishes nothing. The approval is recorded on GitHub beside the run that published, and it holds even when the workflow is started from somewhere other than the skill, so no path publishes unapproved. It exists only if the release publishes from a GitHub Actions workflow rather than from the maintainer's machine, an axis the Publish site and tokens question owns, and it adds an environment and its protection rule to the repository's settings, which nothing in the tree records or checks.
